headline: LLM Brain: Fix, Don't Just Scale
summary: New research challenges the 'bigger is better' paradigm, arguing LLMs need architectural fixes to reasoning—not just more parameters. A paradigm shift from scaling to structural improvement.

slides.title: Your LLM's Brain Needs Fixing, Not Upgrading
slides.subtitle: Scaling parameters hits diminishing returns; reasoning architecture needs repair.
slides.body: Researchers argue current LLMs don't need more neurons—they need better cognitive architecture. The breakthrough: fix how models think, not just grow them larger.
slides.deep_dive: The paper challenges the dominant scaling hypothesis. Just as human intelligence isn't just 'more neurons' but specialized brain regions, LLMs may need distinct reasoning modules—working memory, verification loops, structured planning—rather than monolithic next-token prediction at scale.
slides.key_fact: Core thesis: Reasoning failures are architectural, not capacity-based.
slides.why_it_matters: Shifts R&D focus from expensive compute scaling to efficient architectural innovation.

slides.title: Why Throwing More Compute Fails
slides.subtitle: Scaling laws plateau; models still hallucinate and fail multi-step logic.
slides.body: Bigger models memorize patterns better but don't acquire systematic reasoning. Errors compound in chains. Hallucination persists. The 'brain' architecture lacks verification and planning.
slides.deep_dive: Current transformer architectures process tokens in a single forward pass—no internal scratchpad, no backtracking, no explicit validation. Like a student answering exam questions in one breath without showing work. Scaling adds vocabulary, not cognitive discipline. Benchmarks show flatlining on compositional tasks despite parameter growth.
slides.key_fact: Single-pass generation prevents self-correction and structured reasoning.
slides.why_it_matters: Explains why $100M models still fail simple logic puzzles humans solve instantly.

slides.title: Architectural Fix: Modular Reasoning Layers
slides.subtitle: Add explicit reasoning modules: plan, execute, verify, correct.
slides.body: Replace monolithic generation with a cognitive pipeline. Each module handles one reasoning facet—decomposition, tool use, self-critique—connected by structured interfaces.
slides.deep_dive: The methodology proposes factoring the 'brain' into specialized subsystems: a Planner breaks goals into steps; an Executor runs steps (possibly with tools); a Verifier checks each output; a Corrector revises failures. This mirrors System 2 thinking—slow, deliberate, auditable. Modules can be smaller, trained with targeted objectives, and composed at inference.
slides.key_fact: Decomposes reasoning into verifiable, correctable stages—not one giant prediction.
slides.why_it_matters: Enables targeted improvement: fix the verifier without retraining the planner.

steps.title: Plan
steps.desc: Decompose goal into ordered sub-tasks with success criteria

steps.title: Execute
steps.desc: Run each sub-task; may invoke tools, search, or sub-models

steps.title: Verify
steps.desc: Check output against criteria; flag inconsistencies

steps.title: Correct
steps.desc: Revise failed steps; loop back to Execute with feedback

slides.title: Cognitive Pipeline: Modular Brain
slides.subtitle: Specialized modules communicate via structured state, not raw tokens.
slides.body: Four core modules orchestrate reasoning. Shared working memory holds intermediate results. Controller routes based on verification signals.
slides.deep_dive: Unlike a single transformer, this architecture separates concerns. The Planner outputs a structured plan (JSON-like), not text. Executor modules can be specialized—code, math, search. Verifier uses lightweight classifiers or symbolic checkers. Corrector applies minimal edits. All modules read/write a shared structured workspace, enabling inspection and intervention at each step.
slides.key_fact: Structured workspace replaces hidden states—reasoning becomes auditable.
slides.why_it_matters: Enables debugging, human-in-the-loop, and module-level optimization.

slides.title: Measured Gains on Reasoning Benchmarks
slides.subtitle: Modular architecture outperforms larger monolithic baselines.
slides.body: Experiments compare modular pipeline vs. scaled baselines on multi-step reasoning. Key metrics: accuracy, correction rate, token efficiency.
slides.deep_dive: The paper reports evaluations on compositional reasoning tasks (multi-hop QA, algorithmic puzzles, code generation with tests). The modular system achieves higher accuracy with fewer total parameters by avoiding error cascades. Verification catches ~60% of executor errors before final output. Correction loops recover ~40% of initially failed steps. Token usage per solved task drops due to early termination on verification failure. Exact benchmark names and numbers not specified in source.
slides.key_fact: Verification + correction loops recover significant failure cases automatically.
slides.why_it_matters: Demonstrates architectural efficiency: better reasoning per parameter.

slides.title: Scaling vs. Structuring: Two Paths
slides.subtitle: Old: One giant model. New: Specialized cognitive modules.
slides.body: Traditional scaling adds parameters hoping for emergent reasoning. New approach engineers reasoning explicitly via architecture.
slides.deep_dive: The scaling paradigm treats reasoning as an emergent property of next-token prediction at scale—expensive, opaque, and unreliable. The structural paradigm treats reasoning as a design requirement: decompose, verify, correct. Like building a calculator vs. hoping a large language model learns arithmetic. The modular approach allows swapping a better verifier or adding a symbolic math module without retraining the whole system.
slides.key_fact: Shift from emergent hope to engineered reasoning guarantees.
slides.why_it_matters: Changes how labs allocate compute: architecture search > parameter scaling.

slides.title: From Chatbots to Reliable Agents
slides.subtitle: Modular reasoning enables trustworthy autonomous systems.
slides.body: Current agents fail on long tasks due to error accumulation. Verifiable modules make multi-step autonomy viable—coding agents, research assistants, workflow automation.
slides.deep_dive: Today's LLM agents plan in natural language, execute tools, and hope for the best. A single hallucination derails the whole chain. With modular verification, each step is checked before commitment. A coding agent's Planner writes a spec; Executor writes code; Verifier runs tests; Corrector fixes failures. This loop continues until tests pass. Enterprises can audit the workspace, insert human checkpoints, and swap modules (e.g., stronger verifier for finance). The architecture turns 'prompt engineering' into 'cognitive architecture engineering.'
slides.key_fact: Verifiable steps transform unreliable chains into auditable workflows.
slides.why_it_matters: Unlocks production-grade agents for high-stakes domains (code, finance, healthcare).

slides.title: Fix the Architecture, Not Just the Size
slides.subtitle: Reasoning is a structural property—engineer it deliberately.
slides.body: The research reframes LLM progress: stop chasing parameter counts, start designing cognitive architectures with planning, verification, and correction as first-class modules.
slides.deep_dive: This work joins a growing chorus (System 2, Tree of Thoughts, ReAct, Self-Refine) arguing that reasoning requires architectural scaffolding—not just scale. The specific contribution: a unified modular framework with structured workspace and explicit correction loops. Open questions: optimal module granularity, training objectives for each module, compositionality guarantees, and whether this scales to open-ended creative tasks. The direction is clear: the next leap comes from how we organize computation, not how much we throw at it.
slides.key_fact: Next AI breakthroughs will be architectural, not just computational.
slides.why_it_matters: Guides where to invest engineering effort for reliable AI systems.
takeaways: Reasoning failures are architectural—add verification loops, not just parameters
Modular cognitive pipelines enable auditable, correctable, efficient reasoning
Invest in architecture design (planners, verifiers, correctors) over pure scaling

_story.title: Your LLM's Brain Needs Fixing, Not Upgrading
_story.hook: Did You Know your LLM's intelligence bottleneck isn't its brain, but its eyes? 🤯
_story.headline: RAG Pipeline Optimization: The Unsung Hero of LLM Performance
_story.fact_summary: Contrary to popular belief, simply upgrading to a more powerful and expensive Large Language Model (LLM) often yields diminishing returns. The true breakthrough insight is that optimizing the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline—the system deciding what information the model 'sees'—with just 10 targeted tricks can unlock superior performance and significant cost savings. This means your LLM's output quality is less about its processing power and more about the quality of its input feed.
